title: Thoughts on 'Carnal Knowledge' (1971) by Mike Nicholls?

commenti.body:
Love Carnal Knowledge.

I haven't seen it in a while, but as I remember it, Sandy at the end is no different than Nicholson in the sense that he feeds himself delusional thoughts based on his view of women.

  
I like to see this movie whenever I catch it in the wild, but those scenes with Ann Margaret are just brutal to behold (in a good way of course), so it's probably better I don't see this movie too often.

I just watched it for the first time ever like two months ago.

I think essentially it focuses on the sexual stagnation each character goes through and it's essential effect on them psychologically and as they on in their lives.  That's a simple look at it.

Both of their outlook towards women never gets beyond a shallow stage, even when marriage is involved.  They go through these women as they get on in years but they never evolve past a certain point.  And Jack's character is more severe because for him I don't think it was ever his intent to evolve in the first place, >!at least after the failure of what happened between him and Candace Bergen.  I don't know that he ever dealt with the fact that he used Candace as a prize.  He somehow had real feelings for her mixed up in the betrayal he committed with her against his best friend.  He feels betrayed by her rejection.  He rebels against all of it and becomes promiscuous to the point of shutting down all emotional involvement except for anger and typical misogyny based on his inability to confront his own feelings about it all.  And not only does he never change, he becomes practically impotent w/o orchestrating his own version of how he views himself and sex--which is this ridiculous egotistical script he pays hookers to say so he can get hard, and maybe not even have sex but have power over people he has to pay to be "intimate" with.!<

They both never really evolve with a healthy outlook towards sex, women, relationships etc. and veer off into these alternate husk versions of what they think is an acceptable form of it all.  

So after having been through everything they've been through and getting to the point in their lives they got to, I don't think they learned anything at all.

Yeah it's a pretty interesting film for sure. I too like it and can see myself rewatching it in future. 

> Sandy at the end is no different than Nicholson in the sense that he feeds himself delusional thoughts based on his view of women.

I guess you are right there. He has detoriated too by the end. it's funny that none of the characters we see are successful in relationships. Even the women we come across. Susan is split between the two and for a while is involved with both of them. Then there is Cindy, Sandy's gf in the middle, who has no qualms to see Jonathan secretly. Then there is Bobbie who is not enough for Jonathan and basically forces him into marriage.

Kind of a bleak film tbh even though the tone isn't exactly that.

That's a fine take too. Do you think Susan and Jonathan would have been a successful pairing/marriage?

I also think the women are never fully evolved too. Susan is unsure of what she wants, but we can see that she is quite young. Then there is Cindy who was very interesting but we see little of her. Enough however, to learn that she is not fully into Sandy.

Then there is poor Bobbie who is so desperate for marriage that she lets herself get abused by Jonathan.

I don't think Susan and Jonathan would have been successful because Jonathan pushed it too hard from the outset and his initial get with her was to "win" over Sandy, essentially who would get her in bed first.  And she went along with his pushiness and manipulation, and yes, I think they were all so young when this happened and that's part of their early failures.

I agree that the women didn't evolve really well either.  When the evolution process is interrupted or adjusted in such a way, I think some people never really get the train back on the tracks.  They keep growing but it's a warped growth that isn't natural and they live these altered lives.

The Cindy character was interesting because we don't see much of her.  But coming off of the "free love" movement, much of that attitude seems to excuse the responsibility of human feelings in the name of promiscuity.  Although I'm sure there was healthy sexual freedom, I also think there was open debauchery and hedonism.  It was all commingled as healthy and extremely unhealthy and somewhat impossible for the regular person of the time to navigate.

And yeah, Bobbie let her sexual currency override her individual worth and it got her an unstable, unhealthy relationship.

I think the film is a very real look at human beings trying and failing to navigate human relationships.

> I don't think Susan and Jonathan would have been successful because Jonathan pushed it too hard from the outset and his initial get with her was to "win" over Sandy, essentially who would get her in bed first. And she went along with his pushiness and manipulation, and yes, I think they were all so young when this happened and that's part of their early failures.

I agree. Jonathan is just not equipped for marriage. Why do you feel Susan fell more for Jonathan than Sandy? due to the sex?

> I agree that the women didn't evolve really well either. When the evolution process is interrupted or adjusted in such a way, I think some people never really get the train back on the tracks. They keep growing but it's a warped growth that isn't natural and they live these altered lives.

Well put.

> The Cindy character was interesting because we don't see much of her. But coming off of the "free love" movement, much of that attitude seems to excuse the responsibility of human feelings in the name of promiscuity and infidelity. Although I'm sure there was healthy sexual freedom and it was extremely liberating, I also think there was open debauchery and hedonism. It was all commingled as healthy and extremely unhealthy and somewhat impossible for the regular person of the time to navigate.

That's actually a great insight into this. The movie was made in 1971 and it shows time between 1940-1960 I believe. So viewing it through the sexual freedom lens gives it a lot more sense.

> I think the film is a very real look at human beings trying and failing to navigate human relationships.

Yeah. But weirdly, the film is relatable for the people of that era. I think dynamics before WW2 and 21st century have become quite different to what is portrayed in this film.

It's written by Jules Feiffer who has a uniquely dry and bleak sense of humor. He was a cartoonist, but he also wrote screenplays and plays. Another strange, funny and incredibly bleak movie is Little Murders, based on one of his plays.

> Why do you feel Susan fell more for Jonathan than Sandy? due to the sex?

I don't know that she did.  She spent more time with him, yes, but ultimately she decided to part ways because she wasn't feeling it. 
 He was more persistent, insistent.  And I think the rush of feelings in the beginning was more intense and not necessarily due to the sex.  Sometimes the sex is what breaks it more than what makes it, IMO.  I can't quantify that's what does it in this sense but I don't know that it helped.

Once you can't hide behind words and clothes and it's all out there on the table, the chemistry or lack thereof reveals itself.  It doesn't matter if the physical part is great.  If the feelings aren't there, there's nothing but fleeting pleasure that'll never make up for what doesn't exist.
